title: Task 2 - Checking and correcting
subtitle: Reference words, punctuation and band descriptors
summary: Use the last four minutes well: check your ideas against your plan, fix the verbs and punctuation, and know what separates a Band 6 answer from a Band 8.

lesson.heading: Check the ideas before the spelling
lesson.text: Allow at least **three or four minutes** at the end. Start with the two questions that can still cost you whole bands, then move down to the small errors.

examples.text: **1.** Did you include all of your ideas?
examples.note: Check the answer against the plan you made.

examples.text: **2.** Are your ideas organised and connected logically?
**3.** Then check the verbs, the spelling and the punctuation.

lesson.note: There is rarely time to write an answer and then rewrite it. Spend the time planning at the start and checking at the end instead.

lesson.heading: The phrases doing the work in a good answer
rows: introduce what you want to talk about first
First, let us consider ...
introduce a contrasting idea
however / there is another side to the coin
add a supporting idea
In addition, ...
show you are giving an example
For example, ...
show you are giving a personal opinion
I do think / I believe / As far as I'm concerned
explain the result of an action or situation
Consequently, ...
introduce a summary of your ideas
To summarise, ...

lesson.heading: Reference words hold a paragraph together
lesson.text: Words like *it*, *this*, *these* and *they* refer back to an idea you have already given. They are what stop you repeating a phrase - but each one must point at something the reader can find.

examples.text: *the greatest of **these** is the ease with which it allows us to make contact*
***This** convenience that the internet brings means that our work is only ever a mouse click away*
***These people** end up with more virtual friends than actual friendships*
examples.note: *these people* = users drawn into anti-social behaviour

examples.text: *I believe that **these** can be minimised through education*

lesson.note: If you cannot say what a *this* refers to when you check, the reader will not be able to either. Add the noun after it.

lesson.heading: The errors that survive a first draft
lesson.note: Get to know your own recurring mistakes and practise those deliberately - especially spellings you get wrong more than once.

lesson.heading: Punctuation is marked too
lesson.text: Punctuation errors are counted under Grammatical Accuracy. These are the ones candidates make most.

examples.text: *... more and more**,** it is predicted ...* - a comma splice; use a full stop or *and*.
*Many famous film stars are **american**.* - **American**: nationalities take a capital letter.
*My conclusion**;** therefore is ...* - the semicolon is wrong; use commas: *My conclusion, therefore, is ...*
***the** pie chart gives us ...* - **The**: start a sentence with a capital.
*hours playing video games **which** can lead to health problems* - add a comma before *which*.
*the rate of both **National** and international calls* - **national**: no capital on an ordinary adjective.
*Nowadays**,** in many universities around the world**,** university students ...* - commas around the phrase.

lesson.heading: What the bands actually describe
rows: ideas are clear but there is a lot of repetition
organises information and ideas clearly
uses a wide range of vocabulary fluently and flexibly
only basic vocabulary, used repetitively
an adequate range of vocabulary for the task
a wide range of structures; most sentences accurate
a very limited range of structures, rarely accurate
a mix of simple and complex sentence forms
only very occasional mistakes
frequent spelling mistakes
some errors that do not cause problems for the reader
errors in spelling are rare
lesson.note: The jump from 6 to 8 is not more words - it is **range used accurately**. A complex sentence that goes wrong scores lower than a simple one that does not.

lesson.text: We handwrite less and less these days. Practise writing quickly and neatly, and ask someone else to read what you produce - an answer the examiner cannot read cannot be marked generously.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with what it does in an essay.

pairs.right: introduce what you want to talk about first
explain the result of a situation
introduce a summary of your ideas

exercises.prompt: You have four minutes left. What should you check first?
options: Whether you included all your ideas and organised them logically
exercises.explanation: A missing idea costs Task Response marks that no amount of spelling correction can win back. Check content, then language.

exercises.prompt: Correct the punctuation: *Many famous film stars are ___.*
exercises.explanation: Nationalities take a capital letter. But an ordinary adjective does not - *national and international calls*, lower case.

exercises.prompt: Sort each feature by the band it describes.

items.text: errors may cause problems for the reader
a mix of simple and complex sentence forms
some errors that do not cause problems for the reader
a wide range of vocabulary used fluently and flexibly

exercises.prompt: *I believe that these risks can be ___ through education.* (minimise)
exercises.explanation: *Can be + past participle*. Leaving the verb in its base form after *be* is one of the five commonest verb errors in this task.

exercises.statement: It is better to write a full answer and then rewrite it neatly than to plan first and check at the end.
exercises.explanation: There is rarely time to write twice. Plan at the start, write once, and keep three or four minutes to check.

exercises.prompt: *Many children spend hours playing video games which can lead to health problems.* What is missing?
exercises.explanation: *Which* introduces extra information about the whole idea, so it needs a comma in front of it.

exercises.prompt: What mainly separates a Band 6 answer from a Band 8 answer?
options: Length - Band 8 answers are much longer
A wider range of vocabulary and structures, used accurately
Using more uncommon words, whether or not they are right
exercises.explanation: Range on its own is not enough: Band 8 uses a wide range *and* keeps most sentences accurate.

exercises.prompt: Build a sentence that introduces a contrasting idea in a paragraph.
exercises.answer: Progress comes at a price, however, and there is another side to the coin.
exercises.explanation: *However* in mid-sentence, with commas around it, is a more varied structure than starting every contrast with *However,*.

exercises.statement: If you cannot say what a *this* in your essay refers back to, the reader probably cannot either.
exercises.explanation: Reference words carry the cohesion of a paragraph. When one is vague, add the noun after it - *this convenience*, *these risks*.
